name: bat and ball, faithful case for FALSE

input.proposition: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. So the ball costs 10 cents.
input.text: If the ball were 10 cents the bat would be $1.10 and the pair would come to $1.20, so the ball has to be 5 cents and the bat $1.05.

name: bat and ball, dismissive of the assigned side

input.proposition: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. So the ball costs 10 cents.
input.text: People who say it is not 10 cents are just overthinking a one-line subtraction to look clever.
Let x = 0.999..., then 10x = 9.999..., subtract the first from the second and 9x = 9, so x = 1 exactly.
In a number system that allows infinitesimals, 0.999... can sit an infinitely small amount below 1, so the equality depends on which number system you adopt.

name: falling objects, classic case for TRUE

input.proposition: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones when there is no air.
input.text: Gravity pulls harder on a heavier object, so with nothing to resist it there is more force driving it down, and more force should get it to the ground sooner.

name: falling objects, no argument at all

input.proposition: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones when there is no air.

name: Hamlet, case for TRUE with textual evidence

input.text: He tells Horatio he will put on an antic disposition, and he drops the act whenever he is alone with Horatio or the players, which reads as a plan rather than a breakdown.

name: Hamlet, argues the other side instead

input.text: By act four he is genuinely unstable: he kills Polonius on impulse and turns cruel to Ophelia, so it cannot all be an act.

name: Great Wall, plausible case for TRUE

input.proposition: The Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye.
input.text: The wall runs for thousands of kilometres, and from a low orbit a long, continuous line that contrasts with the terrain can be picked out the way rivers and highways sometimes are.

name: Great Wall, EITHER, picks the distance side

input.proposition: The Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye.
input.text: The wall is only a few metres wide, about the width of a road, so from 400 km up it blends into the hills and no astronaut has reliably picked it out unaided.
